analysis.one_liner: Bans ancestry DNA companies from sharing customers' genetic data with China.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and a subcommittee from October 2023 until the Congress ended, leaving no ban on sending Americans' DNA data to China.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar commercial DNA testing services — companies that sell ancestry and genealogy reports — from disclosing any customer's genetic information to China or to any entity China influences, controls, or owns. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban the same way it enforces rules against unfair or deceptive business practices. The bill was introduced by Rep. Tim Burchett in September 2023 and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers of commercial ancestry and genealogy DNA testing services. Anyone who has mailed a saliva sample to one of these companies would gain a legal guarantee that their genetic information — among the most personal data that exists — could not be handed to China or Chinese-controlled entities, whether deliberately, through a data sale, or through a breach-driven partnership. Because genetic data is shared family data, the protection would also cover relatives who never took a test.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Customers of ancestry DNA testing services

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits commercial DNA testing services from disclosing any individual's genetic information, or aggregates of it, to China or to any entity under China's influence, control, or ownership.

Puts the Federal Trade Commission in charge of enforcement, treating a violation as an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act, so the agency could bring cases and impose penalties against testing companies that send genetic data to Chinese-controlled entities.

analysis.who_pays: The commercial DNA testing industry bears the cost: companies like ancestry and genealogy services would lose the option to share, sell, or partner with Chinese-controlled entities involving customer genetic data, and would face FTC enforcement and penalties if they did. Because the bill defines covered services narrowly as those providing genealogical or ancestry-related information, the burden falls on that specific industry rather than on taxpayers or the general public.

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrow: it covers only services that provide genealogical or ancestry-related information, and only China. It would not restrict sharing genetic data with other foreign governments or entities, and it would not cover genetic data held by health companies, hospitals, or other businesses outside the ancestry-testing definition.

Enforcement depends entirely on the FTC acting case by case under its existing unfair-or-deceptive-practices authority; the bill creates no new monitoring of genetic data flows and gives individuals no stated right to sue a company that discloses their DNA data.

The bill's one-page text imposes a flat prohibition with no compliance safe harbors, leaving companies to guess at what counts as an entity 'under the influence' of China, which an honest supporter would acknowledge creates legal uncertainty for the testing industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its own terms this is a low-cost, targeted privacy rule: it seals off one channel — Chinese state access — through which the genetic data of Americans who bought ancestry tests could leave the country, at the price of foreclosing that market for DNA testing companies. Its real weakness is what it does not do: it protects only ancestry-testing customers, only against China-linked entities, and only as far as FTC enforcement reaches. As a standalone bill it would be a modest step; the stronger criticism is that Congress left even this narrow step unpassed while the consumer genetic-testing industry continued operating under no China-specific disclosure ban.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Burchett introduced the American Genetic Privacy Act of 2023 on September 29, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Six Republican colleagues signed on as cosponsors, bringing total support to seven House Republicans.
On October 6, 2023, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce — the standard path for privacy legislation — and no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, having never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or action in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial DNA testing companies are better off because the bill died: they keep unrestricted freedom to share or sell customer genetic data, including to Chinese-controlled entities, with no FTC prohibition hanging over them. China-linked entities also retain potential access to Americans' genetic data through commercial channels.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: DNA testing companies and China-linked data buyers

for.name: Rep. Tim Burchett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 29, 2023 to ban commercial DNA testing services from disclosing Americans' genetic information to China or Chinese-controlled entities.

for.name: Six Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill after introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 29, 2023 and took no further action on it — no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 6, 2023 and never held a hearing or advanced the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; its seven supporters in the House were all Republicans, and the Republican-run committee that controlled its fate never acted, so no bipartisan or cross-party pattern was ever tested.

industries.industry: Commercial DNA testing companies (ancestry and genealogy services)
industries.note: The bill would bar these companies from disclosing customer genetic information to China or Chinese-controlled entities, cutting off one potential data-sharing or data-sale channel and exposing violators to FTC penalties. Their interest in monetizing customer DNA freely runs directly against the privacy interest of the customers who supplied it.

Entities under the influence, control, or ownership of China would be cut off from lawfully receiving genetic data of U.S. nationals through American commercial testing services. The bill targets exactly this transfer of Americans' most sensitive personal data to foreign state-linked buyers.
